messages.subject: Questions Regarding my Modeling Strategy
messages.body_plain:
Hi All:

I am currently working on a Distance Sampling modeling project as part of
my MS work and had a couple questions:

-Is the "shotgun approach" of looking at all possible model combinations
better, or are there model combinations that are better suited for line
transects (which is how my data was collected?

-I have been adding three series expansions at a time for each analysis.  Are
these each analyzed separately or do each of them additively alter the
result?

Ex.  If I do a Half Normal model of MAWR (Marsh Wren) and select all three
series expansions when I am defining the model would this be three separate
models (HN + Cos, HN + Hermite Polynomial, HN + Simple Polynomial) or would
it be one model (HN + Cos + HP + SP)?

Thanks for reading!

Cheers,
Ben Wishnek

--

messages.subject: Re: Questions Regarding my Modeling Strategy
messages.body_plain:
Ben:

The short answer to your question is to not use the shotgun approach of
all possible model.  If you have a copy of Buckland et al. (2001) at
your disposal, have a look at section 2.4 for a discussion of natural
pairings of key functions and adjustment terms.

The answer to your second question is that you could fit 3 different
models:  half-normal key with cosine adjustment, half-normal key with
Hermite adjustment, half-normal key with simple polynomial adjustment.

messages.subject: multiplier for suitable/potential habitat?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,=20

I feel that my question may have a straightforward answer, so I'm includi=
ng minimal back-story here.=20
I've conducted 212 point count surveys for marsh birds at the landscape s=
cale, replicated 3 times each.  Survey points are reached by, and conduct=
ed from a boat. Detections have been truncated to a 200 meter buffer surr=
ounding each point to avoid overlap in surveyed areas. The issue here is =
concerning "suitable habitat".  As I understand, DISTANCE estimates densi=
ties within the user defined area (200 meter truncation in this case - bi=
rds/hectare). However, since all of these surveys are conducted along a c=
hannel (of varying widths at each point), a portion of the area is not po=
tential habitat.=20

I'm wondering if including the area that IS potential habitat as a point =
transect attribute would be a way to incorporate this into the density es=
timate? Or, if I could simply adjust the estimate to reflect potential ar=
ea after the analysis?  These estimates will be used as the response vari=
able for habitat modeling. This is more of a methods question and possibl=
y out of the realm of this forum, but I could also simply use the "emerge=
nt marsh within 200m" as a predictor variable in the analysis.  I can't w=
rap my head around the best thing to do in this case. Certainly, there ar=
e more elegant ways to do this, but I'm working with the best I have for =
the time being.=20

Thanks in advance for your comments and time.=20
Sincerely,
Ali Leggett

--

messages.subject: Re: multiplier for suitable/potential habitat?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ali, list,

Some unfinished thoughts, but your question really begs for (at least!)=20
2 answers:

1. if you are covering suitable and unsuitable habitat with areas As and=20
Au respectively, and if you assume that density is 0 in unsuitable=20
habitat and Ds in the suitable habitat, then the overall density happens=20
to be D=3D(Ds*As+0*Au)/(As+Au). All else being OK, if you ignore the=20
different densities, D is what you estimate from your distance sampling=20
analysis, so if you want to get density in the suitable area you have to=20
do some simple maths to get it back. The above formula allows you to get=20
Ds from D. But this actually assumes that points are located at random=20
with respect to suitable and unsuitable habitat, which does not seem to=20
be your case, which leads to...

2. the survey you describe is non-standard because the suitable habitat=20
is actually decreasing as a function of distance to the point (because=20
the point is always placed in suitable habitat, right?), so effectively=20
not only detectability is decreasing as a function of distance, but=20
availability of animals decreases as a function of distance. It becomes=20
less clear cut what happens then. Section 6.7 in the introduction to=20
distance sampling book says that if the model you use for the detection=20
function is flexible enough (but that is of course rather vague) then=20
you are modelling the joint effect of detectability and availability=20
(see eq. 6.41 on page 215), and you might still be able to estimate=20
density AT THE POINT. But if that is the case then actually you are=20
estimating Ds directly rather than D, so no correction would be required=20
to estimate Ds.

The problem here is that now the estimated detection function is not=20
simply reflecting detectability, and hence correcting the observed=20
counts to feed into as responses into a model becomes harder to do. If=20
you have the available areas mapped in a GIS you can have some "fun"=20
estimating the true detection function given explicit modelling of e(x)=20
in equation 6.44, and that gets you a step closer to what you need.

hope this helps.

Tiago

messages.subject: analysing aerial survey data in distance
messages.subject_clean: analysing aerial survey data in distance
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

We are trialling an aerial survey technique for seabird surveys across the
ocean.

I have looked at Distance to analyse the data but I am having issues
preparing the data to input, and understanding some of the terminology.

Our survey was conducted at 80m altitude, 80kts speed and we divided the
survey area in to various zones (A,B,C) representing distance from aircraft.

We estimate a 40m band below the aircraft that we cannot survey.

Transects were 60 km long, separated by 2km and there were 21 Transects.

We recorded multi species data, inputted in Excel.  This includes individual
sightings and flocks.

Is there anyone out there who could assist in advising on how to input data
into distance and what we should watch out for?

Thanks

Chris

Dr Chris Surman

messages.subject: Re: analysing aerial survey data in distance
messages.subject_clean: analysing aerial survey data in distance
messages.body_plain:
Chris:

You have a good start on organising your data for analysis.  The
terminology of the way your data were collected is "binned" data, in
that you have distance bands in which your sightings were made rather
than exact distances to the centres of the detected flocks.

I take it from your flight altitude, you know the perpendicular distance
from the flight line to the edges of your three distance bands.  You
will enter the perpendicular distance for detections in Band A as the
average of the perpendicular distances from the two edges of band A (40m
and the outer edge).  You will do the same for the other two bands.
There is a sample Distance project (distributed with the software)
"Ducknest" that shows how binned data are entered.

You can enter all the data from your survey into a single Distance
project, recording the species of birds detected in the "observation
layer" along with the distance band and the size of the cluster
(flock).  You can use the filtering capacity in Distance to analyse
species individually by filtering for observations of "species x".

The other issue for you is the unobservable strip under the plane.
Methods for dealing with this are discussed in Section 7.6.1 of Buckland
et al. (2001) "Introduction to Distance sampling".

One of the challenges of analysing seabird data is their spatial
clustering; some transects may have many flocks, other transects may
have very few (or zero) flocks.  That will make variability between
transects quite high.  But that issue will only become apparent after
you have gotten your data into Distance and begun some exploratory analyses.

If you have further questions, feel free to contact me off list.
